BOOK ENTRY
Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law. It is not a synonym for obedience and does not identify one unchanging class of deeds. The surrounding passage may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the particular acts unnamed. What remains consistent is the rejected claim made for those deeds: they cannot purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The context identifies the work; the phrase denies it as the purchase price.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Rom 3:20, 28; 9:32 KJV/TR; Gal 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) · see The End of the Law

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Romans 3:20 — Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Romans 3:28 — Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
Romans 9:32 — Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;
Galatians 2:16 — Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Galatians 3:2 — This only would I learn of you, Received ye the Spirit by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?
Galatians 3:5 — He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles among you, doeth he it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?
Galatians 3:10 — For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse: for it is written, Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all of Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/48x-the-end-of-the-law.adoc

Paul wrote 1 sentence that has been made to carry a conclusion he spends whole chapters forbidding:

For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.

Read end as termination, and Christ is where the law stops.
Read it as purpose, and Christ is where the law was going.
The English word can carry both senses, and so can the Greek beneath it.
The sentence cannot be settled by the word end alone.
Paul must be permitted to define Paul.

The Greek word is telos: an end, outcome, destination, or goal.
Paul uses it again where no one mistakes it for abolition:

Now the purpose of the commandment is love from a pure heart, from a good conscience, and from sincere faith…
But we know that the law is good if one uses it lawfully.

Love did not terminate the commandment.
Love is what the commandment was designed to produce — “love is the fulfilling of the law” (Romans 13:10).
The same paragraph warns of men who desire to teach the law while understanding neither what they say nor what they affirm; Paul's answer is not that the law is gone, but that it must be used lawfully (1 Timothy 1:7-8).
His next sentence says “the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient” before listing murderers, whoremongers, menstealers, liars, and perjurers (1 Timothy 1:9-10).
The criminal code is laid against the criminal; the righteous man does not need its sentence aimed at him because he is not doing what it condemns.
The verse limits the law's prosecuting office, not its definition of right-living.

Telos can name a resulting destination as well: freed from sin and become servants to God, “ye have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life” (Romans 6:22).
Everlasting life does not abolish the fruit that reaches it.
It is the end toward which that fruit runs.

Romans 10 supplies the same direction.
Israel, Paul says, went about “to establish their own righteousness” and did not submit to “the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).
Christ is then the telos “for righteousness to every one that believeth” — not the end of righteousness, but its embodied aim: God's word believed, obeyed, and lived without defect.
Paul had already closed the abolition reading in the same letter: “Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law” (Romans 3:31).

Christ is not where the law failed and stopped.
He is the word made flesh, the law's right-living purpose made visible, and the pattern into which His people are formed.

Law is not a magic word with 1 referent in every sentence.
Paul regularly attaches a name to it, and the name controls the meaning:

.Paul's named laws and commands

|===
| Phrase | Reference | What governs
| law of God | Romans 7:22, 25; 8:7 | God's instruction, delighted in and served by the inward man
| law of sin | Romans 7:23, 25 | sin ruling the flesh
| law of the Spirit of life | Romans 8:2 | the Spirit's life-giving rule in Christ
| law of faith | Romans 3:27 | the principle that excludes boasting
| law of Christ | Galatians 6:2 | burdens borne in fulfillment of Christ's command
| commandments of God | 1 Corinthians 7:19 | what remains when circumcision and uncircumcision are set aside
| commandments of men | Colossians 2:22; Titus 1:14 | human rules that turn from the truth
|===

The noun law does not erase its modifier.
Freedom from “the law of sin and death” is not freedom from “the law of God” (Romans 8:2; 7:22).
Nor does a human command become disobedience merely because a man gave it.
Paul commands submission to civil rulers (Romans 13:1-7), children to parents, and servants to masters acting within their proper bounds (Ephesians 6:1-8).
A human command becomes a rival command when it conflicts with, replaces, or nullifies what God commanded; then the order is fixed: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Paul has clear vocabulary for the rival register: “traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:14), “tradition of men” (Colossians 2:8), “commandments and doctrines of men” (Colossians 2:22), and “Jewish fables” joined to “commandments of men” (Titus 1:14).
When Paul means God's standard, he is equally plain: “the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good” (Romans 7:12), “the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14), and “I delight in the law of God after the inward man” (Romans 7:22).

Any reading that pours all those laws into 1 bucket will make Paul contradict himself before the page turns.

A work is a deed.
Obedience names the deed's relation to a legitimate command.
The 2 can meet in 1 act without becoming synonyms.

A son who carries his father's message has performed a work and obeyed his father.
The same son may perform the same outward work for his employer without disobeying God; the authorities do not conflict.
Disobedience begins when a command or deed crosses God's command — when a tradition is kept by rejecting what God said (Mark 7:9).

Paul's famous contrast in Romans 4 is not faith against obedience.
He defines the work by its economic claim:

Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.

The picture is a laborer presenting work for wages, making the payer a debtor.
Jesus rules out that claim even after complete obedience: “when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luke 17:10).
Perfect obedience would still create no surplus with which to purchase forgiveness.
The servant has done his duty; the Master owes no wage.

Abraham's faith was not a substitute for obedience.
“By faith Abraham, when he was called… obeyed” (Hebrews 11:8), and James says his faith “wrought with his works” and “by works was faith made perfect” (James 2:22).
His work made faith visible; it did not turn duty into wages.

This is why Paul can write “not of works” and, in the next breath, say we are “created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them” (Ephesians 2:9-10).
Works are excluded as the source and purchase price of the gift, then restored as the life the gift creates.

Paul's other “not of works” sentences keep the same boundary.
Election cannot be earned by children “not yet born, neither having done any good or evil” (Romans 9:11); calling cannot be earned when its purpose and grace were given “before the world began” (2 Timothy 1:9); salvation is “not by works of righteousness which we have done” in the letter that commands believers to “maintain good works” (Titus 3:5, 8).
The excluded works either do not exist yet or cannot purchase the gift; the commanded works follow the gift and show what it produced.

The exact Greek phrase erga nomou, “works of the law,” does not carry 1 hidden code through every occurrence.
Sometimes the context explicitly identifies God's law.
Sometimes the controversy is circumcision and enforced separation.
Sometimes the disputed deed is not named.

Romans 9:32 carries a textual wrinkle worth keeping visible.
The Received Text behind the KJV reads “works of the law.”
The critical Greek text reads simply “as if by works,” without “of the law,” placing still more weight on the attempted manner rather than on a different code.

The Galatian controversy cannot be reduced to “God's commandments are bad works.”
Circumcision was a God-given sign, but the circumcision party turned it into a universal entry requirement and ground of standing.
Paul separates the boundary mark from obedience in 1 sentence: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” (1 Corinthians 7:19).
Galatians 5 makes the disputed use explicit: the man receiving circumcision is seeking to be “justified by the law” (Galatians 5:2-4).
Circumcision itself cannot be the evil, for Paul circumcised Timothy in the next chapter of Acts (Acts 16:3).
The error is demanding the sign as a purchase price and covenant gate God did not set for the nations.

Nor can every occurrence be renamed a commandment of men.
Romans 3 and Galatians 3:10 explicitly identify God's law.
The uniform error lies not in the identity of every deed but in what men demand from it: justification, the Spirit, inheritance, or a boast as though God owed payment.
The law identifies sin and defines right-living; it cannot ransom the man who already broke it, and obedience after the breach cannot turn duty into overpayment.

.Paul's “works of the law” occurrences

|===
| Passage | Classification | Words that decide it
| Romans 3:20, 28 | God's law — clear | The law speaks to the world, gives knowledge of sin, is witnessed by the prophets, and is established in verse 31.
| Romans 9:32, KJV/TR | God's law — clear | Israel pursues “the law of righteousness,” but not by faith, “as it were by works.”
| Galatians 2:16 | Circumcision-party application | Peter separates from Gentiles, fears “them which were of the circumcision,” and compels Gentiles “to live as do the Jews” (Galatians 2:12, 14).
| Galatians 3:2, 5 | Ambiguous acts | The contrast concerns receiving the Spirit by hearing of faith; no disputed act is named, though the letter's live controversy is circumcision.
| Galatians 3:10 | God's law — explicit | Paul writes “the book of the law” and quotes Deuteronomy 27:26: the curse falls on the one who does not continue in what is written “to do them.”
|===

“Ye are not under the law, but under grace” is usually quoted with the next sentence missing.
Paul supplies the forbidden inference himself:

For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.
What then? shall we sin, because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.
Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?

Whatever “not under the law” means, Paul expressly says it cannot mean permission to sin.
The paragraph is about dominion and masters: sin no longer rules; grace receives the servant; obedience runs unto righteousness.
Grace does not leave the man masterless.

Romans 7 uses marriage to make the same point.
Paul says the believer becomes “dead to the law by the body of Christ” so that he may be “married to another… that we should bring forth fruit unto God” (Romans 7:4).
The man dies and changes covenant standing; Paul does not say the law died.
His next question closes that escape: “Is the law sin? God forbid” — then he quotes the tenth commandment, “Thou shalt not covet” (Romans 7:7).
The sequence ends with “the law is holy,” “the law is spiritual,” and “I delight in the law of God” (Romans 7:12, 14, 22).

Romans 8 names the weakness accurately: the law was weak “through the flesh,” so God condemned sin in the flesh “that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit” (Romans 8:3-4).
The Spirit cures the failed walker; He does not erase the right walk.

Galatians says likewise, “if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law” (Galatians 5:18), inside a passage that names adultery, idolatry, hatred, murder, and drunkenness as works of the flesh that exclude from the kingdom (Galatians 5:19-21).
The chapter has just said “all the law is fulfilled in 1 word… Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Galatians 5:14), and it closes the Spirit's fruit with “against such there is no law” (Galatians 5:23).
Led by the Spirit does not mean led into what the law condemns.

Christ redeemed us “from the curse of the law” (Galatians 3:13).
The curse is not the law itself; it is the sentence the law pronounces on the transgressor.
Paul quotes the sentence immediately: “Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them” (Galatians 3:10).
The failure is not obedience but its absence.
Canceling a prisoner's sentence does not repeal the statute he broke.

The law cannot give life to the already dead: “if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law” (Galatians 3:21).
Instruction can identify the right road and convict the man who left it; it cannot raise him from death or pay his debt.
Life remains gift and promise.

Paul then calls the law a paidagōgos, the household custodian who guarded a child until maturity: “the law was our schoolmaster unto Christ… but after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster” (Galatians 3:24-25).
A son who comes of age is no longer under the custodian's hand; he does not therefore become free to steal from his father, dishonor his mother, or worship another god.
The guardian's administration reaches its telos when the Father's instruction is received inwardly and lived by faith.

“The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” is read with the same flattening.
Second Corinthians 3 does not call God's command evil; it contrasts 2 ministrations — “the ministration of condemnation” and “the ministration of righteousness” (2 Corinthians 3:9).
The chapter opens with the Spirit writing, “not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3).
The new covenant does not celebrate an empty heart.
It moves the writing there.

Paul had already asked whether the good commandment was made death to him and answered “God forbid.”
Sin worked death in him “by that which is good,” so that sin might appear exceeding sinful (Romans 7:13).
The letter names and sentences the breach; the Spirit forgives, writes, and empowers the right-living the letter could command but never create.

Hebrews uses the same distinctions in its priesthood argument.
“A change also of the law” is required because “the priesthood” has changed (Hebrews 7:12); the commandment disannulled is the preceding commandment governing mortal Levitical priests, replaced by the power of an endless life (Hebrews 7:16-18).
The meats, drinks, washings, and carnal ordinances imposed until reformation belong to the tabernacle service the chapter is describing (Hebrews 9:1-10).
The new covenant does not leave the heart blank: “I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts” (Hebrews 8:10).
A changed priesthood and an inward writing cannot honestly be summarized as the end of every law.

Ephesians says Christ abolished “the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” (Ephesians 2:15).
The paragraph names its subject before the disputed phrase: circumcision and uncircumcision, aliens and citizens, the “middle wall of partition,” and the making of both peoples into “1 new man” (Ephesians 2:11-19).
Whatever the ordinances include, the thing Christ kills is the enmity that keeps the nations apart.
The same letter later quotes the fifth commandment — “Honour thy father and mother” — and calls it “the first commandment with promise” (Ephesians 6:2).
Paul cannot mean that every commandment was abolished in chapter 2 and binding in chapter 6.

Colossians does not say the Torah was nailed to the cross.
It says God forgave trespasses by blotting out a singular cheirographon, a handwritten debt-record “that was against us” (Colossians 2:13-14).
The hostile document matches the debt canceled; nomos, law, never appears in the sentence.
When the chapter later identifies the ordinances to which the Colossians must not submit, it quotes them — “Touch not; taste not; handle not” — and names their source: “the commandments and doctrines of men” (Colossians 2:20-22).

The command concerning feast, new moon, and sabbath is not stop keeping them but “let no man therefore judge you” (Colossians 2:16).
Paul calls them things which “are a shadow of things to come” — present shadow, coming referent — and a shadow is not an enemy of its body but the outline cast by it (Colossians 2:17).
The verse may govern how the days are judged; it does not announce their abolition.

Galatians 4 is equally specific about the road being retraced.
Its readers formerly “did service unto them which by nature are no gods,” and Paul asks why they turn “again to the weak and beggarly elements” before naming “days, and months, and times, and years” (Galatians 4:8-10).
Gentiles cannot return to a Mosaic calendar they never kept.
At minimum, the verse cannot bear the claim that every appointed time of God has ended while its own word “again” points backward to pagan bondage.

Romans 14 names neither sabbath nor unclean animals.
Its dispute is between one who eats all things and a weak brother who “eateth herbs,” and it later adds wine (Romans 14:2, 21).
The word translated “unclean” in verse 14 is koinos, common, not akathartos, the law's word for an unclean animal.
The chapter governs doubtful disputes, private esteem, and care not to destroy a brother over food; an unnamed day and a vegetarian's conscience cannot repeal a named command.

Acts 15 likewise begins with the stated claim “Except ye be circumcised… ye cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1).
The council refuses circumcision as the purchase price of covenant entry, gives the nations 4 necessary commands drawn from the law, and then observes that Moses “is read in the synagogues every sabbath day” (Acts 15:20-21).
Paul afterward circumcises Timothy for the Jews, hastens to be at Jerusalem for Pentecost, and publicly demonstrates that the report he teaches Jews to forsake Moses is false: “thou thyself also walkest orderly, and keepest the law” (Acts 16:3; 20:16; 21:21-24).
Those acts do not settle every command's application to every covenant member, but they forbid turning Paul into a witness that God's law was evil or dead.

Paul's own verdict remains the safest reading rule:

Do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid: yea, we establish the law.

The end of the law is love from a pure heart, right-living formed in those who walk after the Spirit, and Christ Himself — the Word believed, the command obeyed, the Father's character made visible.
He is not the law's funeral.
He is its purpose.
